answer.rationale: Three converging signals: a recent release, climbing p99 on the write path, and peak settlement traffic. Memory b1 (day 18) is the only archived precedent for a checkout-error class incident resolving via rollback of a release, with the prior build confirmed stable and rollback completing without customer impact. That makes rollback the lowest-risk single intervention that matches both the recent-deploy cause model and the preservation of write availability at peak. Verifying b1 before committing is cheap insurance against misapplying an outdated precedent, since it is the foundational rule of the rollback playbook. Other directions are ruled out for this single-action window: a regional failover (memory b2) addresses regional latency recovery, not a release regression on the write path; read-replica routing (b5) offloads reads but does not protect writes, which is the explicit primary objective; circuit breakers (b4) and capacity (b3) are useful second-window actions if rollback does not stabilize p99, but neither matches the recent-release correlation as directly. Note: rollback carries a non-zero cost in the form of lost in-flight writes during the deploy swap; if the source record for b1 surfaces any caveat about that risk on peak days, I will reconsider failover or circuit breaking before acting.
